title: Where did these sayings come from?

entries.note: A word first used by [[see:William Shakespeare]], mentioned in passing because the hosts say number idioms are countless.
Painting pre-drawn pictures by matching numbered paint pots; an American craze of the 1940s and '50s invented by [[see:Max S. Klein]] and [[see:Dan Robbins]].
Michigan engineer credited with inventing [[see:painting by numbers]] kits.
Artist credited alongside [[see:Max S. Klein]] with inventing [[see:painting by numbers]].
To trick or fool someone; origin unknown, possibly vaudevillian, where a number is a song, or perhaps boxing; compared with British [[equivalent:stitch someone up]].
British expression Rob uses to explain [[equivalent:do a number on someone]]; Jess has heard it but doesn't use it.
To have worked someone out, knowing them so well you'd know their phone number.
Newspapers applied it to [[see:Al Capone]], but [[see:J. Edgar Hoover]]'s FBI officially gave it first to [[see:John Dillinger]] in 1934.
American gangster arguably the first [[see:public enemy number one]], since a newspaper dubbed him that.
First official [[see:public enemy number one]], shot by officers outside a Chicago cinema after a cigar-lighting signal in 1934.
Designated [[see:John Dillinger]] [[see:public enemy number one]] in 1934.
The third person lighting a cigarette from one match gets bad luck, supposedly from wartime snipers spotting, aiming and firing at successive lights.
Origin uncertain: perhaps a lottery or draft number, or biblical passages about the number of one's days, such as [[from?:Job 38:21]].
To be number one is called too obvious to need explaining, like other number-one idioms.
One of several number-one idioms the hosts call self-explanatory.
One of several number-one idioms the hosts call self-explanatory.
One of the number-two idioms Jess found self-explanatory.
To reach the right conclusion from the evidence, as opposed to [[see:put two and two together and make five]].

entries.term: put two and two together and make five
entries.note: To reach the wrong conclusion from the evidence; an extension of [[from:put two and two together]].
A self-explanatory number-two idiom that refers to no particular game.
A number-two idiom that does refer to a specific dance.
Also care two hoots: to care two of a tiny amount, since a [[from:hoot]] meant the smallest imaginable quantity.
Long used for the smallest imaginable amount, as in 'not worth a hoot in Hades' (1923); Jess had assumed a minced oath or hooting and hollering.
Cited as the unsplittable smallest particle, by comparison with [[see:hoot]] as the smallest amount.
Perhaps doubling [[from?:a penny for your thoughts]], the biblical widow's two coins, a gambler's bets or the [[see:two-penny post]].
A 16th-century expression; [[see:two cents]] may be a doubling of it.
British 'my two penn'orth', a contraction of two pennies' or tuppence worth, possibly predating [[same-root?:two cents]].
Early English postage cost two pennies, a weakly supported explanation of [[see:two cents]].
From the older [[from:third time is lucky]], reflecting a cultural sense that three makes a complete sequence or structure.
The older version of [[gave:third time's the charm]].
The idea that groups of three feel satisfying, memorable or complete, as in [[see:friends, Romans, countrymen]] or [[see:stop, drop and roll]].
An example of the [[see:rule of three]].

entries.term: life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness
entries.note: An example of the [[see:rule of three]].
An example of the [[see:rule of three]].
A reminder that three can be one too many, contrasting with the [[see:rule of three]].
Raised as a proverb that runs against [[see:third time's the charm]].
His speech in Hamlet is full of famous sayings that amount to empty, self-contradictory advice, like the clashing proverbs about three.
A night so cold you need three dogs sleeping beside you, said to be Inuit or Australian Aboriginal; poorly evidenced, and repeated by the band [[see:Three Dog Night (band)]].
A band whose widely repeated story spread the explanation of [[see:three dog night]].
Listed in the Oxford Dictionary of Idioms; Rob says it simply refers to maps having four corners.
Formerly meant equal to or an exact analogy with; neither host has heard that use, and today it suggests being demeaned or sexualised.
To give someone a bunch of fives is to punch them, with a hand of five digits.
Like [[see:bunch of fives]], refers to the five fingers of the hand.
Another way of asking for a [[equivalent:high five]].
Stealing, with your five fingers as the discount card.
A punishment, from English boys' schools where it meant six strokes of the cane.
The devil's number, or number of the beast, from the beast of Revelation in most New Testament manuscripts and translations.
Refers to grave depth; neither UK nor US law requires six feet, but the practice dates to at least the 16th century as a plague precaution.
Slang from [[from:Skrilla]]'s song 'Doot Doot (6 7)', spread through clips of 6'7" [[see:LaMelo Ball]] and a viral '67 kid'; unrelated to [[unrelated:at sixes and sevens]].
Confused or disorganised, from the older dice phrase [[from:set on six and seven]]; Francis Grose (1785) applied it to scattered furniture and unsettled business.
To risk everything, probably from dice; used by Chaucer in Troilus and Criseyde, and the source of [[gave:at sixes and sevens]].

entries.term: six of one and half a dozen of the other
entries.note: Rob suspects its sense of ambivalence colours his reading of [[see:at sixes and sevens]].
Rapper whose song 'Doot Doot (6 7)' repeats six seven as a hook, the supposed origin of [[see:67]].
NBA player, 6'7" tall, whose viral clips helped spread [[see:67]].
Jess's favourite variation of [[from:67]], related to 'getting sendy', as in send it.
From the Abrahamic idea of seven layers of heaven, the top one housing God and the angels; already in use in Old English.
Greek astronomy's seven classical planets helped make seven significant, and ultimately gave the [[gave:seven-day week]] and its day names.
Derived from the [[from:Ptolemaic system]]'s seven planets; French keeps Mars, Mercury, Jupiter and Venus day names where English went Germanic.
Seven is the most likely total with two six-sided dice, as six combinations produce it.
Thoroughly, in every direction, or in a frantic state; dates to the early 1700s with no good explanation found; also [[equivalent:seven ways to Sunday]].
A variant of [[equivalent:six ways from Sunday]].
Another variant of [[equivalent:six ways from Sunday]].
Covered in the nautical idioms episode; untied sails flapping around uncontrollably, like a drunk person.
Drunk, from the received wisdom that you could drink eight beers and be fine, but one more would intoxicate you.
Losing, from pool: behind the eight ball you have no shot that isn't a foul; compared with British [[equivalent:snookered]].
The British snooker equivalent of [[equivalent:behind the eight ball]].
Restless desire for change after seven years of marriage, transferred from an itch such as scabies said to recur for seven years.
Magic boots covering seven leagues a stride, found in European fairy tales, most famously stolen from an ogre in [[see:Charles Perrault]]'s [[see:Hop-o'-My-Thumb]].
Author of [[see:Hop-o'-My-Thumb]], the most famous tale featuring [[see:seven-league boots]].
Perrault's tale of a tiny, wise youngest of seven children who steals an ogre's [[see:seven-league boots]].
Another sign that fairy tales favour sevens, like the seven children in [[see:Hop-o'-My-Thumb]].
Covered in the hosts' second idioms episode; supposedly from a Wiltshire regiment noted for its smart appearance.
Covered before; from cloud altitude classifications, nine being very high; the phrase has also been [[equivalent:on cloud seven]].
An earlier variant of [[equivalent:cloud nine]].
Origin uncertain: a 19th-century anecdote about a judge's giant shirt, fighter-jet ammunition belts (which popularised it), kilt length, or concrete trucks.

entries.term: a stitch in time saves nine
entries.note: A small early repair prevents a bigger one; nine may mean nine stitches or simply rhyme with time.
Recorded in John Heywood's 1546 proverbs; Spanish cats have seven lives, as in [[see:Siete vidas]]; a link to [[see?:Bastet]] is poorly evidenced.
Spanish TV show set in Madrid, named because Madrid people are nicknamed [[see:los gatos]] and Spanish cats have seven lives.
Nickname for the people of Madrid, explaining the title [[see:Siete vidas]].
Egyptian goddess suggested, with little evidence, as the source of [[see:cats have nine lives]].

entries.term: possession is nine-tenths of the law
entries.note: Whoever physically holds something has the advantage; from at least the 1800s, preceded by the 17th-century [[from:possession is eleven points of the law]].
A plainer way of saying [[equivalent:possession is nine-tenths of the law]].

entries.term: possession is eleven points of the law
entries.note: A 17th-century proverb, out of a supposed twelve points, the forerunner of [[gave:possession is nine-tenths of the law]]; the twelve points are unexplained.
A base-ten idiom that needs no explanation.
Feeling successful or confident; only dated to the 1950s, though 'ten-foot' meant very big much earlier, as in [[see:ten-foot coal]].
Term for particularly thick Yorkshire coal deposits, not literally ten-foot seams.

entries.term: wouldn't touch with a 10 ft pole
entries.note: Originally a [[from:40 ft pole]], then a [[see:barge pole]]; earliest pole references date to the mid-1800s; see also the Grinch's 39½-foot pole.
The earliest length in the idiom, later shortened to [[gave:wouldn't touch with a 10 ft pole]].
British variant, 'wouldn't touch with a barge pole': a pole 8–16 feet long used to push barges through bridge tunnels.

entries.term: not to be handled with a pair of tongs
entries.note: Dates to 1643; the OED suggests a link to Envy's long tongs of hatred in Chaucer's [[see?:The Parson's Tale]].
Chaucer tale in which Envy holds a hot iron to the heart with long tongs, possibly behind [[see?:not to be handled with a pair of tongs]].
Possibly from Spanish [[from?:tan galán]] or a Spanish word for hat trim; it holds only three-quarters of a gallon.
Spanish modifier, as in 'un sombrero tan galán', a very fine hat; a proposed source of [[gave?:10-gallon hat]].
The classic cowboy hat, named after 19th-century hat maker [[from:John Batterson Stetson]]; its ads showed a cowboy watering his horse from one.
From [[from:Spinal Tap]]'s amp dial going to 11; Jess compares Chico Marx answering '11' in [[see:Duck Soup]].
The film whose 'this one goes up to 11' gave [[gave:turn it up to 11]].
Marx Brothers film where Chico answers '11' when asked for 1 to 10, compared with [[see:turn it up to 11]].
Thirteen: bakers added a loaf so a dozen met legal weight requirements, given harsh punishments for underweight bread; also [[equivalent:devil's dozen]].
A past name for thirteen, like [[equivalent:baker's dozen]].
Another past name for thirteen, like [[equivalent:baker's dozen]].
Thirteen; the hosts guess an extra copy covered faulty pages, as with [[equivalent:baker's dozen]].
Inflated from the [[from:$64 question]], probably via [[see:The $64,000 Question]], and later to the [[gave:million-dollar question]].
The original idiom, from the top prize on the 1940s CBS radio quiz [[from:Take It or Leave It]].
1940s CBS radio quiz show whose $64 top prize gave the [[gave:$64 question]].
A further inflation of the [[from:$64,000 question]], now followed by the billion- and even trillion-dollar question.
1950s quiz show, presumably exaggerating the [[see:$64 question]], infamous for contestants being fed answers; [[see:Patty Duke]] testified in an inquiry.
Made famous by [[see:The $64,000 Question]]; Jess covered its origin on her Substack and blog.
Appeared on [[see:The $64,000 Question]] and testified in a televised Senate inquiry into the quiz-show scandals.
Means I love you, from the letters in each word, as used by [[see:Fred Rogers]] on Mr. Rogers' Neighborhood.
Used [[see:143]] for I love you on Mr. Rogers' Neighborhood and reportedly kept his weight at 143 lb for 30 years.
Social-media numeric code for I love you forever, extending [[see:143]].
Eight letters, three words, one meaning: I love you, from a 2001 Lisa Stansfield song chorus.
A nap; 40 simply meant a big number, as in [[see:40 days and 40 nights]]; earliest citation in William Kitchiner's long-titled book.
Jesus's time in the desert, cited as biblical evidence that 40 meant a big number in [[see:40 winks]].
Used to mean sleep long before the phrase [[see:40 winks]].
